title: Characterizing nonunitary quantum space
formal: Do the matrix-problem characterizations of bounded-error unitary quantum space extend to quantum space with intermediate nonunitary operations? For every space-constructible integer function \(s(n)\) satisfying \(s(n)=\Omega(\log(n+2))\) and \(s(n)\le n^{O(1)}\), the precise class-equality formulation is \[\mathrm{BQSPACE}(s)=\mathrm{BQ}_{U}\mathrm{SPACE}(s).\] The two classes below allow \(O(s(n))\) workspace and \(2^{O(s(n))}\) computation steps, with acceptance thresholds \(2/3\) and \(1/3\). The right-hand class permits only unitary gates before its final measurement. Equality transfers the source's complete matrix problems to the general class under the same reductions. This historical question was resolved affirmatively at STOC 2021.

why: The result identifies the role of measurement when memory is scarce: allowing intermediate measurements does not enlarge bounded-error quantum space. It also makes the source’s concrete matrix problems complete for the general computational model, connecting limited-memory quantum computation to numerical linear algebra.
status_note: Resolved affirmatively by Fefferman–Remscrim, STOC 2021 Theorem 1. On 16 September 2026 the original question 3 and matrix definitions/completeness statements, full later model definitions, logarithmic-space argument, general-space theorem and padding proof were checked. The class equality transfers the existing matrix characterizations to general nonunitary space. The repaired source selection was explicitly authorized by the user. sentences: The question concerns quantum computation with a limited workspace and intermediate measurements.
The original source asks whether matrix problems characterizing unitary quantum space also characterize this more general model.
A 2021 theorem proves that intermediate measurements do not increase bounded-error decision power at any space-constructible bound at least logarithmic.
The simulation retains space proportional to the original bound when running time is at most exponential in that bound.
This resolves the title-matching question; the erroneous quotation about interactive proofs has been replaced and the completed historical card belongs in the archive.

definitions:
A promise problem is a pair \((L_{\mathrm{yes}},L_{\mathrm{no}})\) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings. The input is \(x\), and \(n=|x|\). Correctness is required only on the promised inputs. The function \(s\) is space-constructible: a deterministic Turing machine can mark out \(s(n)\) work cells on an input of length \(n\), using \(O(s(n))\) workspace. Logarithms are base two. Bounds hide constants fixed for the machine and problem, independent of \(x\). A read-only input tape and write-only output tape are not counted as workspace; all retained measurement outcomes and other working classical information are counted.

Use the uniform circuit convention of the resolution paper. A deterministic classical Turing machine generates the complete description of the circuit for \(x\) using \(O(s(n))\) workspace and at most \(2^{O(s(n))}\) steps. The circuit has \(h=O(s(n))\) qubits, at most \(2^{O(s(n))}\) gates, and starts in \(|0^h\rangle\). A qubit has state space \(\mathbb C^2\); the full register has dimension \(d=2^h\). A mixed state is a positive semidefinite Hermitian \(d\)-by-\(d\) matrix of trace one. Here Hermitian means \(A=A^\dagger\), with dagger denoting conjugate transpose, and positive semidefinite means \(v^\dagger A v\ge0\) for every vector \(v\).

For the unitary class, each gate is from the fixed universal set consisting of Hadamard, CNOT and T, acting on its designated wires: \[H=2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\quad \mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\oplus c\rangle.\] Here \(b,c\in\{0,1\}\), \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two, and \(i^2=-1\). There are no intermediate measurements. If \(U_x\) is the circuit product and \(\Pi_1\) projects onto value one of its output qubit, its acceptance probability is \(\operatorname{Tr}(\Pi_1 U_x|0^h\rangle\langle0^h|U_x^\dagger)\). The problem belongs to \(\mathrm{BQ}_{U}\mathrm{SPACE}(s)\) when this probability is at least \(2/3\) on every yes-input and at most \(1/3\) on every no-input.

For the general class, each gate is a quantum channel \(\Phi:\operatorname{Mat}(d)\to\operatorname{Mat}(d)\), a complex-linear map that is trace-preserving and completely positive. Complete positivity requires \(\Phi\otimes I_r\) to preserve positive semidefiniteness for every auxiliary dimension \(r\). Intermediate measurement with its outcome retained in work qubits, outcome-dependent later operations, and resetting work qubits are allowed. There is no free external store of outcomes. For exact finite descriptions, follow Definitions 6–7 of the resolution paper: vectorizing matrices in a fixed row order gives a \(d^2\)-by-\(d^2\) matrix \(K(\Phi)\) satisfying \(\operatorname{vec}(\Phi(A))=K(\Phi)\operatorname{vec}(A)\). Its entries are Gaussian rationals \((a+ib)/c\), with integers \(a,b,c\), \(c>0\), in binary. The uniform generator outputs these entries for every channel, within its total resource bound. This bound limits their bit lengths; there are no noncomputable numerical constants. All described gates are promised to be valid channels. The final state is \(\Phi_t\circ\cdots\circ\Phi_1(|0^h\rangle\langle0^h|)\), and its acceptance probability is the trace against \(\Pi_1\). The same yes/no thresholds define \(\mathrm{BQSPACE}(s)\). Fixed-gate and rational-channel conventions describe bounded-error classes; approximation is allowed within the fixed acceptance gap and does not require exact equality of individual output distributions.

The source's matrix tasks use succinct row encodings: an input of length \(n\) describes a deterministic algorithm that lists all nonzero entries and column indices of any requested row in polynomial time and \(O(s(n))\) workspace. Matrix dimension is \(2^{O(s(n))}\), so the full matrix need not fit in the input. The well-conditioned inversion task distinguishes \(|H^{-1}_{u,v}|\le a\) from \(|H^{-1}_{u,v}|\ge b\), for fixed \(0\le a<b\le1\), with positive definite \(H\) satisfying \(\kappa^{-1}I\preceq H\preceq I\) and a given \(\kappa=2^{O(s(n))}\). The minimum-eigenvalue task distinguishes \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\le a\) from \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\ge b\), for positive semidefinite \(H\) with bounded entries and a promised gap at least \(2^{-O(s(n))}\). Outside these promises no answer is required. The source proves both tasks complete for unitary space using classical polynomial-time, \(O(s(n))\)-space reductions. Completeness means membership plus reductions from every problem in the class, preserving yes- and no-instances. Equality of the two classes therefore gives the same hardness and membership for nonunitary space, without changing the matrix tasks.
answer_criterion: The retained mathematical target is a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed equality for every admissible \(s\), together with its consequence that the source's complete matrix problems characterize the general class under the original reductions. It suffices to formalize the general-to-unitary containment and the existing unitary characterizations; bounded-error unitary computations already fit the general model. The published STOC 2021 Theorem 1 proves the equality for every space-constructible \(s=\Omega(\log n)\), including the entire range used here. This source-based resolution is the reason for archival; this review does not claim to have supplied a Lean formalization. A simulation using one new qubit for every measurement would not give the required space bound. No polynomial-time bound in the original running time alone is required, no exact preservation of every output probability is claimed, and the adjacent interactive-proof question is outside this target.

context_blocks.text: The imported title referred to nonunitary quantum space, but its quotation came from the preceding question about exponentially small gaps in interactive proofs. On 16 September 2026 the user selected the title-matching target. The citation is therefore repaired to §6 question 3; no claim is made here about PreciseQIP versus PSPACE.

Unitary computation preserves the full quantum state until the final measurement. General computation can measure, forget information and reuse its workspace. Storing every measurement outcome would postpone measurement, but can consume space proportional to running time rather than to the original workspace.

The 2018 source gives complete well-conditioned matrix-inversion and minimum-eigenvalue problems for unitary quantum space. Its open question asks whether analogous hardness results hold when nonunitary operations are permitted. Equality of the two space classes is a sufficient—and, with these complete tasks, equivalent—way to answer this question.

Fefferman and Remscrim prove \(\mathrm{BQ}_{U}\mathrm{SPACE}(s)=\mathrm{BQSPACE}(s)\) for every space-constructible \(s=\Omega(\log n)\). Their Theorem 1 also covers space-bounded quantum witness classes. Its special case \(s=\Theta(\log n)\) identifies general quantum logspace with unitary quantum logspace. The published theorem supplies the positive answer retained here.

For a computation using space \(s\) and time \(t\), the resolution paper discusses simulation in space \(O(s+\log t)\) and time polynomial in \(t2^s\). Under the class convention \(t=2^{O(s)}\), this remains \(O(s)\) space and \(2^{O(s)}\) time. This resource statement does not promise time polynomial in \(t\) independently of \(s\).

The result concerns bounded-error decision power with classical uniform control. It does not assert that every physical channel can be implemented exactly by a unitary on the same register, or that irreversible dynamics disappear. These distinctions are compatible with equality of the computational classes.
